<reflection>
After two experiments (high and low catalyst), the fitting results show that M3 (dimer catalysis) has the lowest NLL, closely followed by M12, M9, M10, M15, M1, and M2. M5 and M4 are ruled out due to very high NLL. The top candidates include mechanisms with dimerization (M3, M2), simple Michaelis-Menten (M1), and deactivation (M9, M10, M12, M15). The aim of the previous turn was to discriminate between activation/lag and bimolecular scaling; the low-catalyst experiment ruled out M5 and M6/M8 (which have higher NLL), but the remaining candidates are still closely clustered. My aim for this turn is to design an experiment that distinguishes between deactivation by product (M12) and other mechanisms, and also tests the dimer catalysis (M3) versus monomer catalysis (M1/M2).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
2. Hypothesis discrimination: The key differences among the leading candidates are:
   - M12 involves irreversible deactivation by product (P + cat → inactive_catP). Adding product should accelerate deactivation, leading to an early plateau and lower final conversion.
   - Other deactivation mechanisms (M9, M10, M15) do not involve product in deactivation, so added product will only affect reversibility and equilibrium, not deactivation rate.
   - M3 involves catalysis by the dimer (cat2), while M1 and M2 involve catalysis by monomer. At intermediate catalyst concentrations, the effective active species differs, affecting the rate law.
   - M1 and M2 are reversible Michaelis-Menten, so added product will slow the initial rate and shift equilibrium.

3. Discriminative experiment design: Propose an experiment with moderate catalyst (0.01 M), the same substrate concentration (2.0 M) to maintain consistency, and a significant initial product concentration (0.2 M). This will test the effect of product on deactivation and reversibility without saturating the system.

4. Contrastive predictions:
   - M12: Added product will accelerate deactivation, causing the reaction to slow down prematurely and plateau at a conversion lower than the equilibrium conversion predicted by reversibility alone. The time course may show an early inflection.
   - M9, M10, M15: Deactivation is independent of product, so the curve will resemble that without added product but with a slower initial rate due to reversibility. Final conversion may be reduced by deactivation, but not additionally by product-accelerated deactivation.
   - M1, M2: No deactivation; the curve will be slower due to reversibility, and final conversion will be determined by equilibrium (possibly lower due to added product). No early plateau beyond equilibrium.
   - M3: Similar to M1/M2 in terms of reversibility, but the rate law may differ due to dimer catalysis. The initial rate may be lower relative to M1/M2 if dimerization is less favorable at this catalyst concentration.
   These differences will be evident in the shape of the product vs. time curve, particularly in the final conversion and the presence of an early plateau.
</hypothesis>
